title: Elevation and micro-scale environmental variables shape ant taxonomic and functional diversity along an elevational gradient
content:
Abstract
Mountain grassland habitats host high biodiversity and are considered vulnerable. Ants are important ecological indicators and their communities respond to elevation as well as small-scale environmental variables. As such, they represent an ideal taxon to disentangle the contribution of different-scale environmental drivers on biodiversity patterns. Although several studies have investigated some of these aspects, most of them included different habitats, and only a few of them were performed in Europe. We investigated ant taxonomic and functional diversity and community composition in grasslands along an elevational gradient in 2 mountains of the Apennines (Italy). We found that elevation and vegetation height negatively affected ant taxonomic and functional diversity, while ant functional diversity was higher in east-facing plots. Ant taxonomic community composition was shaped by elevation but also by vegetation height, rock cover, and east-facing aspect. On the other hand, ant functional community composition was driven by elevation, litter and rock cover, vegetation height, and both north- and east-facing aspects. Altogether, our results show that ant diversity and community composition respond to both elevation and small-scale environmental variables that act as environmental filters.
